newsitem.title: UK: British parliament cast changes,but same director.
newsitem.headline: British parliament cast changes,but same director.

text.p: Former showgirl Betty Boothroyd was chosen by a radically changed British parliament on Thursday to be its mistress of ceremonies, but admitted she would have trouble identifying most of the cast.

Boothroyd's re-election as speaker came in the first sitting of the House of Commons since the sensational May 1 election when Tony Blair's Labour Party stormed into power with an overall majority of 179.

The political earthquake which ended 18 years of Conservative rule brought some 260 new MPs into the 659-member House -- a fact which Boothroyd, once a member of the Tiller Girls, a high kicking dance troupe, said would give her initial problems.
"I hope soon to be able to put a name to every face, but they (new members) will understand, I am sure, that it will be difficult to achieve this in a short period of time," she said.

In the last parliament, Boothroyd, 67, was a minor celebrity in the United States where Prime Minister's question time, with its sharp confrontations which she refereed, was a favourite among viewers of one cable TV channel.

"There is no doubt at all who is the star of that show," new Prime Minister Blair told her after she had been elected. "It is not the then leader of the opposition, or the then prime minister. It is yourself."
In the last parliament, in which the Conservatives eventually lost their overall majority, Boothroyd was forced to give a casting vote in one particularly close division.

But Blair predicted that her services as a tie-breaker were unlikely to be needed again. "I hope I will not be accused of complacency if I say it (the casting vote) should not be repeated in this parliament," he said to laughter.
The scene as parliament re-assembled after the election was transformed from the the dying days of the administration of Conservative John Major a few short weeks ago.
Most of the 418 Labour members packed into the benches to Boothroyd's right which are traditionally occupied by government supporters while others stood or sat in the gangways or on crossbenches.
The previous sprinkling of women members among them was now a flood, following a temporary change in Labour party rules to provide for all-women candidates shortlists in many constituencies.
One member, Ann Begg, sat in a wheelchair, the first British MP to be so disabled.

On the opposition side of the House, the depleted ranks of the Conservatives -- down to 165 members -- were joined by rows of Liberal Democrats after the minority party more than doubled its representation at the election to 46. Martin Bell, a BBC journalist who became Britain's first independent MP for decades after fighting on an anti-corruption platform, sat among the throng wearing a white suit -- ever his trade mark when he reported from world trouble spots.
